title: Same Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Different Treatment: Tumour Biology Decides Who Needs Chemotherapy
excerpt: Two women in their 50s with similar-sized tumours diverge on a single HER2 test — one avoids chemotherapy, the other needs it plus targeted therapy, oncologist Dr Nisha Shariff explains.
body:
• Two women in their 50s with similar-sized, hormone receptor-positive tumours can get different treatment: HER2-negative disease is treated with surgery, radiotherapy and hormone therapy, while HER2-positive disease adds chemotherapy and HER2-targeted therapy.
  • Ask for three results before comparing your plan with anyone else's: oestrogen/progesterone receptor status, HER2 status, and tumour grade and stage — plus whether genomic testing can show if chemotherapy is likely to help you.
  • Almost half of breast cancers in Malaysia are diagnosed at stage III or IV; get any new lump, skin dimpling, nipple change or persistent redness checked promptly — most lumps are not cancer, but only assessment can tell.
  • 'Aggressive' describes how fast a cancer may grow, not your personal outcome: HER2-positive cancer once carried a poor prognosis, but targeted therapy has transformed survival for many women.

Two women receive the same words — breast cancer — and leave the clinic with different treatment plans. Consultant clinical oncologist Dr Nisha Shariff at Sunway Medical Centre, Sunway City, uses that contrast to explain modern care: breast cancer is not one disease, and tumour biology, not tumour size alone, decides who needs chemotherapy. Her account was reported by Business Today Malaysia and in detail by PP Health Malaysia.

"What may look similar on paper can behave very differently. Understanding what is driving the cancer helps us determine which treatment is most appropriate for each patient. We are not simply treating breast cancer; we are treating the person and their specific type of cancer."

— Dr Nisha Shariff, Consultant Clinical Oncologist, Sunway Medical Centre

How biology splits one diagnosis into different paths

Doctors classify tumours by whether they carry oestrogen or progesterone receptors, whether they overproduce the HER2 protein that drives cell growth, and by grade and stage. Hormone receptor-positive cancers can be slowed by hormone therapy. HER2-positive cancers need HER2-targeted medicines, usually with chemotherapy. Triple-negative cancers have none of those markers, so chemotherapy, immunotherapy or other medicines carry more of the load.

Dr Nisha's example makes the split concrete, as Parenthood Malaysia also reported: two women in their 50s with similar-sized hormone receptor-positive tumours diverge on one test. The HER2-negative patient follows surgery, radiotherapy and hormonal therapy. The HER2-positive patient follows the same base and adds chemotherapy plus HER2-targeted treatment. Age, general health, menopausal status and personal preference then adjust the plan further.

Context: genomic testing and the word 'aggressive'

Genomic testing examines tumour features to estimate whether chemotherapy is likely to add benefit, so some patients can safely avoid it and others do not miss it. That is the practical question behind the headline: chemo is added when biology predicts benefit, not by default for every diagnosis.

The word 'aggressive' needs the same care. HER2-positive and triple-negative cancers can grow faster than other subtypes, but faster growth does not fix an individual outcome. HER2-positive disease is the clearest proof — once a poor-prognosis subtype, it now responds to targeted therapy that has, in Dr Nisha's words, transformed outcomes and improved survival in many women. Stage, grade, receptor status and response to treatment tell you more than the label alone.

What to do with this information

Do not measure your treatment against a friend's or relative's. Ask instead: What is my ER, PR and HER2 status? What is my stage and grade? Has genomic testing been considered for the chemotherapy decision? What support exists beyond the tumour — for fertility, body confidence, work and emotional wellbeing — since multidisciplinary teams now plan for survivorship, not only for treatment?

Screening remains the lever patients control. In Malaysia, breast cancer is the most common cancer among women and almost half of cases — roughly 1 in 2 — are found at stage III or IV, when options narrow. A mammogram can find changes before symptoms appear; ultrasound helps assess lumps and dense tissue, and MRI is reserved mainly for higher-risk women. Seek assessment for a new lump in the breast or armpit, a change in size or shape, skin dimpling or thickening, persistent redness or swelling, a newly inverted nipple, unusual discharge, a persistent nipple rash or sore, or localised pain that does not settle — even if your last mammogram was normal.

What's next

No new drug is announced in these reports. The change is in decision-making: receptor and genomic results first, treatment second. For diaspora readers navigating care in the US, India or Malaysia, the actionable step is identical — bring the full pathology report to the consultation and ask how each result changed the plan. If the answer is only the stage, ask again about biology.
